# Writing migrations

A migration is a Go file. `makemigrations` writes it, and after that it is
yours: you can read it in code review, edit it, reorder it, and add
operations it could never have guessed.

```go
// Generated by gormgate 0.1.0 on 2026-09-23 07:07

package migrations

import (
	m "github.com/ctolon/gormgate/migrations"
)

func init() {
	m.Register(&m.Migration{
		App:  "blog",
		Name: "0002_post_views",
		Dependencies: []m.Key{
			{App: "blog", Name: "0001_initial"},
		},
		Operations: []m.Operation{
			&m.AddField{
				ModelName: "post",
				Name:      "views",
				Field: m.Field{
					Type:      m.Int,
					Size:      64,
					DBDefault: m.DBValue(int64(0)),
				},
			},
		},
	})
}
```

`init()` registers it. That is the whole mechanism: because Go has no
runtime import, a migration has to be compiled into your command, and
`makemigrations` maintains `cmd/gorm-gate/zz_gormgate_migrations.go` so that
it is.

!!! warning "Rebuild after editing"
    The migrations the tool sees are the ones in the binary. `go run
    ./cmd/gorm-gate` rebuilds every time, so this is usually invisible — but
    if you run a pre-built binary, rebuild it after writing or editing a
    migration. gormgate notices the mismatch and refuses to run rather than
    migrating a history it cannot see.

## The fields of a migration

| Field | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `App`, `Name` | Identify it. `Name` is the file name without `.go`. |
| `Dependencies` | Migrations that must be applied first, in this app or another. |
| `Operations` | What it does, in order. |
| `Initial` | Marks the first migration of an app, which is what `--fake-initial` may skip. |
| `Atomic` | Overrides whether it runs in a transaction, where the database has them. |
| `Replaces` | Set by `squashmigrations`: the migrations this one stands in for. |
| `RunBefore` | Migrations that must run *after* this one, for a dependency you cannot express from the other side. |

## The operations

**Models** — `CreateModel`, `DeleteModel`, `RenameModel`, `AlterModelTable`,
`AlterModelTableComment`, `AlterUniqueTogether`, `AlterModelOptions`.

**Fields** — `AddField`, `RemoveField`, `AlterField`, `RenameField`.

**Indexes and constraints** — `AddIndex`, `RemoveIndex`, `RenameIndex`,
`AddConstraint`, `RemoveConstraint`, `AlterConstraint`.

**Special** — `RunSQL`, `RunGo`, `SeparateDatabaseAndState`.

Every operation knows how to describe itself, how to change the project
state, and — where it can — how to reverse itself, which is what makes
`migrate <app> <earlier>` work.

## Adding an index by hand

```go
&m.AddIndex{
	ModelName: "post",
	Index: m.Index{
		Name:   "idx_post_author_created",
		Fields: m.Columns("author_id", "created_at"),
	},
},
```

`m.Columns` is shorthand for the common case. Spell the elements out when
you need more than a column name:

```go
Fields: []m.IndexField{
	{Column: "created_at", Sort: m.SortDesc},
	{Expression: "lower(title)"},
},
```

Indexes can also carry `Where` (a partial index), `Include` (covering
columns), `OpClasses` and `Type` — each supported by the databases that have
it, and rejected with a clear error by the ones that do not. See
[Databases](../vendors.md).

## Running SQL

```go
&m.RunSQL{
	SQL:        m.Script("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm"),
	ReverseSQL: m.Script("DROP EXTENSION IF EXISTS pg_trgm"),
},
```

`SQL` is one of three things, and the compiler will not let it be anything
else:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `m.Script("...")` | a script, which the backend splits into statements the way its own client would |
| `m.Statements("a", "b")` | statements, each run as it is |
| `m.Parameterized{{SQL: "... ?", Params: []any{1}}}` | statements with values bound to their placeholders |

Use `m.NoSQL` as `ReverseSQL` for something that needs no undoing — without
a reverse, the migration cannot be unapplied at all.

`RunSQL` changes the database but not gormgate's idea of the schema. If your
SQL does something the state should know about, wrap the pair:

```go
&m.SeparateDatabaseAndState{
	DatabaseOperations: []m.Operation{&m.RunSQL{SQL: m.Script("...")}},
	StateOperations:    []m.Operation{&m.AddIndex{ /* ... */ }},
},
```

That is also how you tell gormgate "this already exists, just record it".

## An empty migration to write into

```console
$ go run ./cmd/gorm-gate makemigrations blog --empty --name add_trigram_index
```

## Dependencies between apps

The autodetector works these out for you — a model with a foreign key to
another app's model gets a dependency on that app's migration. When you need
one by hand:

```go
Dependencies: []m.Key{
	{App: "blog", Name: "0001_initial"},
	{App: "auth", Name: "__first__"},
},
```

`__first__` and `__latest__` mean what they say, and survive the other app
gaining migrations later.

## Reversibility

`migrate blog 0001` unapplies everything after `0001`. An operation that
cannot be reversed — a `RunSQL` with no `ReverseSQL`, a `RunGo` with no
`ReverseCode` — stops that, and the error names the operation and the
migration so you know which one to give a reverse.
